questions.question_text: A paper dipped in a dil. $H_{2}SO_{4}$ solution of ' $X$ ' upon treatment with $SO_{2}$ gas turns into green. The compound ' $X$ ' is :
questions.question_html: A paper dipped in a dil. $H_{2}SO_{4}$ solution of ' $X$ ' upon treatment with $SO_{2}$ gas turns into green. The compound ' $X$ ' is :
questions.explanation_text: The correct answer is Option D: $K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}$ . A paper dipped in dilute $H_{2}SO_{4}$ solution of $X$ turns green when treated with $SO_{2}$ gas. This means that $X$ must be a substance which changes to green on reduction by $SO_{2}$ . Now, $SO_{2}$ is a reducing agent . Acidified potassium dichromate, that is, $K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}$ in dilute $H_{2}SO_{4}$ , is orange in colour and gets reduced to $Cr^{3+}$ , which is green . The reaction is: $Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}+3SO_{2}+2H^{+} \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+}+3SO_{4}^{2-}+H_{2}O$ So, the orange dichromate paper turns green. Now check other options briefly: A: $KI$ -starch This is used to detect oxidising agents; it gives blue colour due to iodine-starch complex, not green. B: $KMnO_{4}$ Acidified $KMnO_{4}$ gets decolourised by $SO_{2}$ , not green. C: $Pb(CH_{3}COO)_{2}$ Lead acetate paper is used for detecting $H_{2}S$ , giving black colour. Hence, the compound $X$ is $K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}$
questions.explanation_html:
The correct answer is Option D: $K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}$ .

A paper dipped in dilute $H_{2}SO_{4}$ solution of $X$ turns green when treated with $SO_{2}$ gas.

This means that $X$ must be a substance which changes to green on reduction by $SO_{2}$ .

Now, $SO_{2}$ is a reducing agent.

Acidified potassium dichromate, that is, $K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}$ in dilute $H_{2}SO_{4}$ , is orange in colour and gets reduced to $Cr^{3+}$ , which is green.

The reaction is:

$Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}+3SO_{2}+2H^{+} \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+}+3SO_{4}^{2-}+H_{2}O$

So, the orange dichromate paper turns green.

Now check other options briefly:

  • A: $KI$ -starch

    This is used to detect oxidising agents; it gives blue colour due to iodine-starch complex, not green.

  • B: $KMnO_{4}$

    Acidified $KMnO_{4}$ gets decolourised by $SO_{2}$ , not green.

  • C: $Pb(CH_{3}COO)_{2}$

    Lead acetate paper is used for detecting $H_{2}S$ , giving black colour.

Hence, the compound $X$ is

$K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}$

questions.explanation_text: Statement A $Mo(VI)$ and $W(VI)$ are less stable than $Cr(VI)$ . This statement is incorrect . In group 6 elements: $Cr$ , $Mo$ and $W$ commonly show the $+6$ oxidation state. The higher oxidation states become more stable for heavier members of the group. So, $Cr(VI)$ is strongly oxidising and less stable comparatively, while $Mo(VI)$ and especially $W(VI)$ are more stable . Hence, A is false . Statement B $Ce^{4+}$ and $Tb^{4+}$ are oxidant while $Eu^{2+}$ and $Yb^{2+}$ are reductant. This statement is correct . Reason: $Ce^{4+}$ tends to change to $Ce^{3+}$ , so it acts as an oxidising agent . $Tb^{4+}$ also tends to reduce to $Tb^{3+}$ , so it is an oxidant . $Eu^{2+}$ tends to change to $Eu^{3+}$ , so it donates electrons and acts as a reducing agent . $Yb^{2+}$ similarly tends to go to $Yb^{3+}$ , so it is also a reductant . Hence, B is true . Statement C Cm and Am have seven unpaired electrons. This statement is incorrect . Let us see the electronic configurations: $Am$ : $[Rn]5f^{7}7s^{2}$ $Cm$ : $[Rn]5f^{7}6d^{1}7s^{2}$ Now count unpaired electrons: In $Am$ , $5f^{7}$ gives 7 unpaired electrons In $Cm$ , $5f^{7}$ gives 7 unpaired , and $6d^{1}$ gives 1 more unpaired So $Cm$ has 8 unpaired electrons , not 7. Hence, C is false . Statement D Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction. This statement is correct . Reason: In actinoids, the $5f$ electrons shield the nuclear charge even more poorly than the $4f$ electrons do in lanthanoids. Therefore, the decrease in atomic and ionic size across actinoids is greater . Hence, D is true . Final conclusion Correct statements are: $B\text{and}D\text{only}$ So the correct option is: $\text{Option C}$
questions.explanation_html:
Statement A

$Mo(VI)$ and $W(VI)$ are less stable than $Cr(VI)$ .

This statement is incorrect.

In group 6 elements:

  • $Cr$ , $Mo$ and $W$ commonly show the $+6$ oxidation state.

  • The higher oxidation states become more stable for heavier members of the group.

So,

  • $Cr(VI)$ is strongly oxidising and less stable comparatively,

  • while $Mo(VI)$ and especially $W(VI)$ are more stable.

Hence, A is false.

Statement B

$Ce^{4+}$ and $Tb^{4+}$ are oxidant while $Eu^{2+}$ and $Yb^{2+}$ are reductant.

This statement is correct.

Reason:

  • $Ce^{4+}$ tends to change to $Ce^{3+}$ , so it acts as an oxidising agent.

  • $Tb^{4+}$ also tends to reduce to $Tb^{3+}$ , so it is an oxidant.

  • $Eu^{2+}$ tends to change to $Eu^{3+}$ , so it donates electrons and acts as a reducing agent.

  • $Yb^{2+}$ similarly tends to go to $Yb^{3+}$ , so it is also a reductant.

Hence, B is true.

Statement C

Cm and Am have seven unpaired electrons.

This statement is incorrect.

Let us see the electronic configurations:

  • $Am$ : $[Rn]5f^{7}7s^{2}$

  • $Cm$ : $[Rn]5f^{7}6d^{1}7s^{2}$

Now count unpaired electrons:

  • In $Am$ , $5f^{7}$ gives 7 unpaired electrons

  • In $Cm$ , $5f^{7}$ gives 7 unpaired, and $6d^{1}$ gives 1 more unpaired

So $Cm$ has 8 unpaired electrons, not 7.

Hence, C is false.

Statement D

Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction.

This statement is correct.

Reason:

  • In actinoids, the $5f$ electrons shield the nuclear charge even more poorly than the $4f$ electrons do in lanthanoids.

  • Therefore, the decrease in atomic and ionic size across actinoids is greater.

Hence, D is true.

Final conclusion

Correct statements are:

$B\text{and}D\text{only}$

So the correct option is:

$\text{Option C}$

questions.question_html:
Consider the following statements about manganate and permanganate ions. Identify the correct statements.

A. The geometry of both manganate and permanganate ions is tetrahedral.

B. The oxidation states of Mn in manganate and permanganate are +7 and +6, respectively.

C. Oxidation of Mn(II) salt by peroxodisulphate gives manganate ion as the final product.

D. Manganate ion is paramagnetic and permanganate ion is diamagnetic.

E. Acidified permanganate ion reduces oxalate, nitrite and iodide ions.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :

questions.explanation_text: Manganate ion $\rightarrow MnO_{4}^{-2}$ Permanganate ion $\rightarrow MnO_{4}^{-}$ (A) In both ions, Mn is surrounded by four oxygen atoms. So, the shape of both $MnO_{4}^{-2}$ and $MnO_{4}^{-}$ is tetrahedral (often written as $d^{3}s$ hybridisation in this context). (B) For $MnO_{4}^{-}$ , let oxidation state of Mn be $x$ . Then $x+4(-2)=-1 \Rightarrow x=+7$ . For $MnO_{4}^{-2}$ , $x+4(-2)=-2 \Rightarrow x=+6$ . So, Mn is $+7$ in permanganate and $+6$ in manganate (the statement given is reversed). (C) When $Mn^{2+}$ salt is oxidised by peroxodisulphate $S_{2}O_{8}^{2-}$ , the product formed is permanganate ion, not manganate: $Mn^{2+}+S_{2}O_{8}^{2-} \rightarrow MnO_{4}^{-}$ (Permanganate ion) (D) In $MnO_{4}^{-}$ , Mn is in $+7$ state, which corresponds to $3d^{0}$ (no unpaired electrons), so it is diamagnetic. In $MnO_{4}^{-2}$ , Mn is in $+6$ state, which corresponds to $3d^{1}$ (one unpaired electron), so it is paramagnetic. (E) Acidified permanganate ion acts as a strong oxidising agent, so it oxidises (i.e., “reduces” itself while oxidising) oxalate, nitrite and iodide ions.
questions.explanation_html:
Manganate ion $\rightarrow MnO_{4}^{-2}$

Permanganate ion $\rightarrow MnO_{4}^{-}$

(A) In both ions, Mn is surrounded by four oxygen atoms. So, the shape of both $MnO_{4}^{-2}$ and $MnO_{4}^{-}$ is tetrahedral (often written as $d^{3}s$ hybridisation in this context).

(B) For $MnO_{4}^{-}$ , let oxidation state of Mn be $x$ . Then $x+4(-2)=-1 \Rightarrow x=+7$ .

For $MnO_{4}^{-2}$ , $x+4(-2)=-2 \Rightarrow x=+6$ .

So, Mn is $+7$ in permanganate and $+6$ in manganate (the statement given is reversed).

(C) When $Mn^{2+}$ salt is oxidised by peroxodisulphate $S_{2}O_{8}^{2-}$ , the product formed is permanganate ion, not manganate:

$Mn^{2+}+S_{2}O_{8}^{2-} \rightarrow MnO_{4}^{-}$ (Permanganate ion)

(D) In $MnO_{4}^{-}$ , Mn is in $+7$ state, which corresponds to $3d^{0}$ (no unpaired electrons), so it is diamagnetic.

In $MnO_{4}^{-2}$ , Mn is in $+6$ state, which corresponds to $3d^{1}$ (one unpaired electron), so it is paramagnetic.

(E) Acidified permanganate ion acts as a strong oxidising agent, so it oxidises (i.e., “reduces” itself while oxidising) oxalate, nitrite and iodide ions.

questions.question_text: On heating a mixture of common salt and $K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}$ in equal amount along with concentrated $H_{2}SO_{4}$ in a test tube, a gas is evolved. Formula of the gas evolved and oxidation state of the central metal atom in the gas respectively are:
questions.question_html: On heating a mixture of common salt and $K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}$ in equal amount along with concentrated $H_{2}SO_{4}$ in a test tube, a gas is evolved. Formula of the gas evolved and oxidation state of the central metal atom in the gas respectively are:
questions.explanation_text: Gas evolved is chromyl chloride , formed in the chromyl chloride test . Step 1: Reaction (NCERT) On heating $K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}$ with a chloride salt (common salt $NaCl$ ) and conc. $H_{2}SO_{4}$ , red fumes of chromyl chloride are obtained: $K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}+4NaCl+6H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow 2CrO_{2}Cl_{2}+2KHSO_{4}+4NaHSO_{4}+3H_{2}O$ So, the gas is $CrO_{2}Cl_{2}$ . Step 2: Oxidation state of Cr in $CrO_{2}Cl_{2}$ Let oxidation state of Cr be $x$ . Oxygen: $2 \times (-2)=-4$ Chlorine: $2 \times (-1)=-2$ Sum = $x-4-2=0$ $x-6=0 \Rightarrow x=+6$ Correct option Option C: $CrO_{2}Cl_{2}$ and +6
questions.explanation_html:
Gas evolved is chromyl chloride, formed in the chromyl chloride test.

Step 1: Reaction (NCERT)

On heating $K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}$ with a chloride salt (common salt $NaCl$ ) and conc. $H_{2}SO_{4}$ , red fumes of chromyl chloride are obtained:

$K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}+4NaCl+6H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow 2CrO_{2}Cl_{2}+2KHSO_{4}+4NaHSO_{4}+3H_{2}O$

So, the gas is $CrO_{2}Cl_{2}$ .

Step 2: Oxidation state of Cr in $CrO_{2}Cl_{2}$

Let oxidation state of Cr be $x$ .

  • Oxygen: $2 \times (-2)=-4$

  • Chlorine: $2 \times (-1)=-2$

Sum = $x-4-2=0$

$x-6=0 \Rightarrow x=+6$

Correct option

Option C: $CrO_{2}Cl_{2}$ and +6

questions.question_text: Consider the following reactions : $\begin{aligned} & NaCl+K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}+H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow A+KHSO_{4}+NaHSO_{4}+H_{2}O \\ & A+NaOH \rightarrow B+NaCl+H_{2}O \\ & B+H_{2}SO_{4}+H_{2}O_{2} \rightarrow C+Na_{2}SO_{4}+H_{2}O \end{aligned}$ In the product ' $C^{'}$ , ' $X$ ' is the number of $O_{2}^{2-}$ units, ' $Y$ ' is the total number oxygen atoms present and ' $Z$ ' is the oxidation state of $Cr$ . The value of $X+Y+Z$ is $____$ .
questions.question_html:
Consider the following reactions :

$\begin{aligned} & NaCl+K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}+H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow A+KHSO_{4}+NaHSO_{4}+H_{2}O \\ & A+NaOH \rightarrow B+NaCl+H_{2}O \\ & B+H_{2}SO_{4}+H_{2}O_{2} \rightarrow C+Na_{2}SO_{4}+H_{2}O \end{aligned}$

In the product ' $C^{'}$ , ' $X$ ' is the number of $O_{2}^{2-}$ units, ' $Y$ ' is the total number oxygen atoms present and ' $Z$ ' is the oxidation state of $Cr$ . The value of $X+Y+Z$ is $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: The first reaction is the well-known Chromyl chloride test . When a chloride salt like sodium chloride ( $NaCl$ ) is heated with potassium dichromate ( $K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}$ ) and concentrated sulfuric acid ( $H_{2}SO_{4}$ ), deep red vapors of chromyl chloride are evolved. $4NaCl+K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}+6H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow 2CrO_{2}Cl_{2}+2KHSO_{4}+4NaHSO_{4}+3H_{2}O$ Thus, Product A is Chromyl chloride ( $CrO_{2}Cl_{2}$ ) . When chromyl chloride gas is passed through an aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide ( $NaOH$ ), a yellow solution of sodium chromate is formed. $CrO_{2}Cl_{2}+4NaOH \rightarrow Na_{2}CrO_{4}+2NaCl+2H_{2}O$ Thus, Product B is Sodium chromate ( $Na_{2}CrO_{4}$ ) . When a solution of a chromate acts with hydrogen peroxide ( $H_{2}O_{2}$ ) in an acidic medium (provided by $H_{2}SO_{4}$ ), a deep blue-colored compound known as chromium pentoxide is formed. $Na_{2}CrO_{4}+H_{2}SO_{4}+2H_{2}O_{2} \rightarrow CrO_{5}+Na_{2}SO_{4}+3H_{2}O$ Thus, Product C is Chromium pentoxide ( $CrO_{5}$ ) . Chromium pentoxide has a famous "butterfly structure". Finding $X$ : In its structure, there are two peroxide ( $O-O$ ) linkages. Each peroxide linkage represents one $O_{2}^{2-}$ unit. Therefore, the number of $O_{2}^{2-}$ units is $2$ . So, $X=2$ . Finding $Y$ : The chemical formula is $CrO_{5}$ , meaning there are $5$ oxygen atoms in total. So, $Y=5$ . Finding $Z$ : Out of the $5$ oxygen atoms in the butterfly structure, one is bonded by a double bond (normal oxide with an oxidation state of $-2$ ), and the remaining four form the peroxide linkages (with an oxidation state of $-1$ each). Let the oxidation state of Chromium ( $Cr$ ) be $Z$ . We can calculate it as follows: $Z+1(-2)+4(-1)=0$ $Z-2-4=0$ $Z=+6$ So, $Z=6$ . $\therefore$ $X+Y+Z=2+5+6=13$
questions.explanation_html:
The first reaction is the well-known Chromyl chloride test. When a chloride salt like sodium chloride ( $NaCl$ ) is heated with potassium dichromate ( $K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}$ ) and concentrated sulfuric acid ( $H_{2}SO_{4}$ ), deep red vapors of chromyl chloride are evolved.

$4NaCl+K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}+6H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow 2CrO_{2}Cl_{2}+2KHSO_{4}+4NaHSO_{4}+3H_{2}O$

Thus, Product A is Chromyl chloride ( $CrO_{2}Cl_{2}$ ).

When chromyl chloride gas is passed through an aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide ( $NaOH$ ), a yellow solution of sodium chromate is formed.

$CrO_{2}Cl_{2}+4NaOH \rightarrow Na_{2}CrO_{4}+2NaCl+2H_{2}O$

Thus, Product B is Sodium chromate ( $Na_{2}CrO_{4}$ ).

When a solution of a chromate acts with hydrogen peroxide ( $H_{2}O_{2}$ ) in an acidic medium (provided by $H_{2}SO_{4}$ ), a deep blue-colored compound known as chromium pentoxide is formed.

$Na_{2}CrO_{4}+H_{2}SO_{4}+2H_{2}O_{2} \rightarrow CrO_{5}+Na_{2}SO_{4}+3H_{2}O$

Thus, Product C is Chromium pentoxide ( $CrO_{5}$ ).

Chromium pentoxide has a famous "butterfly structure".

  • Finding $X$ : In its structure, there are two peroxide ( $O-O$ ) linkages. Each peroxide linkage represents one $O_{2}^{2-}$ unit. Therefore, the number of $O_{2}^{2-}$ units is $2$ .

    So, $X=2$ .

  • Finding $Y$ : The chemical formula is $CrO_{5}$ , meaning there are $5$ oxygen atoms in total.

    So, $Y=5$ .

  • Finding $Z$ : Out of the $5$ oxygen atoms in the butterfly structure, one is bonded by a double bond (normal oxide with an oxidation state of $-2$ ), and the remaining four form the peroxide linkages (with an oxidation state of $-1$ each).

    Let the oxidation state of Chromium ( $Cr$ ) be $Z$ . We can calculate it as follows:

    $Z+1(-2)+4(-1)=0$

    $Z-2-4=0$

    $Z=+6$

    So, $Z=6$ .

$\therefore$ $X+Y+Z=2+5+6=13$

Statement II : There is increase in the concentration of reactants on the surface of catalyst which strengthens the bonds in reacting molecules. questions.question_html:
Given below are two statements for catalytic properties of transition metals.

Statement I : First row transition metals which act as catalyst utilise their 3d electrons only for formation of bonds between reactant molecules and atoms on the surface of catalyst.

Statement II : There is increase in the concentration of reactants on the surface of catalyst which strengthens the bonds in reacting molecules.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
options.html: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

options.label: B
options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
options.html: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect

options.label: C
options.text: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
options.html: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect

questions.explanation_text: The first-row transition metals use both their 3d and 4s electrons to form bonds with reactant molecules on the surface of the catalyst. ∴ Statement I is incorrect. When reactants are adsorbed on the catalytic surface, their concentration on the surface increases, but this adsorption actually weakens the bonds within the reactant molecules. This helps in forming an activated complex and reduces the activation energy of the reaction. ∴ Statement II is incorrect.
questions.explanation_html:
The first-row transition metals use both their 3d and 4s electrons to form bonds with reactant molecules on the surface of the catalyst.

∴ Statement I is incorrect.

When reactants are adsorbed on the catalytic surface, their concentration on the surface increases, but this adsorption actually weakens the bonds within the reactant molecules. This helps in forming an activated complex and reduces the activation energy of the reaction.

∴ Statement II is incorrect.

options.html: They have high melting points, higher than those of pure metals.

options.label: B

questions.explanation_text: The main physical and chemical properties of interstitial compounds are : (1) They have very high melting points, even higher than the pure metals from which they are formed. (2) They are extremely hard. For example, some borides can be almost as hard as diamond. (3) They continue to show metallic conductivity, meaning they can conduct electricity like metals. (4) They are chemically inactive (inert) and often do not have a fixed composition, which is called being non-stoichiometric.
questions.explanation_html:
The main physical and chemical properties of interstitial compounds are :

(1) They have very high melting points, even higher than the pure metals from which they are formed.

(2) They are extremely hard. For example, some borides can be almost as hard as diamond.

(3) They continue to show metallic conductivity, meaning they can conduct electricity like metals.

(4) They are chemically inactive (inert) and often do not have a fixed composition, which is called being non-stoichiometric.

questions.explanation_html:
Statement I

An ion is coloured in aqueous solution if it has partially filled $d$ -orbitals (so that $d\text{-}d$ transitions are possible). Ions with $d^{0}$ or $d^{10}$ configurations are colourless.

Now check each pair:

  1. $[Sc^{3+},Ti^{3+}]$

  • $Sc^{3+}$ : Sc $(Z=21)$ is $[Ar]3d^{1}4s^{2}$ ; so $Sc^{3+}=[Ar]3d^{0}$ (colourless)

  • $Ti^{3+}$ : Ti $(Z=22)$ is $[Ar]3d^{2}4s^{2}$ ; so $Ti^{3+}=[Ar]3d^{1}$ (coloured)

    $\Rightarrow$ Both not coloured

  1. $[Mn^{2+},Cr^{2+}]$

  • $Mn^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{5}$ (coloured)

  • $Cr^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{4}$ (coloured)

    $\Rightarrow$ Both coloured ✅

  1. $[Cu^{2+},Zn^{2+}]$

  • $Cu^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{9}$ (coloured)

  • $Zn^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{10}$ (colourless)

    $\Rightarrow$ Both not coloured

  1. $[Ni^{2+},Ti^{4+}]$

  • $Ni^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{8}$ (coloured)

  • $Ti^{4+}=[Ar]3d^{0}$ (colourless)

    $\Rightarrow$ Both not coloured

So, the number of pairs in which both ions are coloured is only $1$ , not $3$ .

Hence, Statement I is false.

Statement II

A reducing agent is a species that gets oxidised (it donates electrons).

  • $Ce^{4+}$ is a well-known strong oxidising agent (it gets reduced to $Ce^{3+}$ ).

  • $Th^{4+}$ is also in a high oxidation state and is not a strong reducing agent.

  • $Gd^{3+}$ is a very stable common oxidation state for Gd; not strongly reducing.

  • $Eu^{2+}$ readily gets oxidised to $Eu^{3+}$ , so it acts as a strong reducing agent among the given species.

Therefore, the strongest reducing agent among $Th^{4+},Ce^{4+},Gd^{3+}$ and $Eu^{2+}$ is $Eu^{2+}$ , not $Th^{4+}$ .

Hence, Statement II is false.

Correct Option

Since both Statement I and Statement II are false, the correct choice is:

Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.explanation_text: A. Mn forms the oxide $Mn_{2}O_{7}$ , in which Mn is in its highest oxidation state. To find the oxidation state of Mn in $Mn_{2}O_{7}$ , we set the sum of oxidation states to zero. Let Mn's oxidation state be 'x'. Oxygen's oxidation state is typically -2. $2(\text{x})+7(-2)=0$ $2\text{x}-14=0$ $2\text{x}=14$ $\text{x}=+7$ Manganese is a Group 7 element with an electronic configuration of $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{2}$ . The highest possible oxidation state for manganese is +7, which involves the loss of all 7 valence electrons. Therefore, Mn is indeed in its highest oxidation state (+7) in $Mn_{2}O_{7}$ . This statement is correct . B. Oxygen stabilizes the Mn in higher oxidation states by forming multiple bonds with Mn. In high oxidation states, transition metals strongly attract electrons, increasing the covalent character of their bonds with oxygen. This is particularly true for elements like Mn in a +7 oxidation state. The formation of multiple bonds (e.g., Mn=O) allows for better delocalization of electron density, which helps to stabilize the high positive charge on the central metal atom. This is a common phenomenon for high oxidation state metal oxides (e.g., $CrO_{3}$ , $V_{2}O_{5}$ ). This statement is correct . C. $Mn_{2}O_{7}$ is an ionic oxide. Ionic oxides are typically formed when the metal has a low oxidation state and a significant electronegativity difference with oxygen leads to electron transfer (e.g., $MnO$ ). However, as the oxidation state of a metal increases, its ability to polarize electron clouds increases, and the covalent character of its bonds with oxygen becomes prominent. $Mn_{2}O_{7}$ is a dark green, viscous liquid with a melting point of -20 °C. These properties are characteristic of a molecular covalent compound, not an ionic solid which would have a high melting point. It is highly covalent due to the high electronegativity of oxygen and the high charge density of $Mn^{7+}$ . Therefore, $Mn_{2}O_{7}$ is a covalent oxide, not an ionic oxide. This statement is incorrect . D. The structure of $Mn_{2}O_{7}$ consists of one bridged oxygen. The structure of $Mn_{2}O_{7}$ can be represented as $O_{3}Mn-O-MnO_{3}$ . It consists of two $MnO_{4}$ tetrahedra sharing a common oxygen atom. The oxygen atom that links the two manganese atoms is a bridging oxygen. Each Mn atom has three terminal oxygen atoms and one bridging oxygen atom. This statement is correct . Based on the analysis, statements A, B, and D are correct, while statement C is incorrect. The final answer is $\text{B}$

• Cr (Z = 24):

  • Mn (Z = 25):

    Ground state configuration:

    $Mn:[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{2}$

First ionisation enthalpy, $\Delta_{i}H_{1}$

In the first ionisation process:

  • Cr:

    $Cr \rightarrow Cr^{+}+e^{-}$

    $Cr^{+}:[Ar]3d^{5}$ (a very stable half-filled configuration)

  • Mn:

    After removal of one 4s electron:

    $Mn^{+}:[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}$ (not as stable as half-filled 3d⁵ only)

Because the resulting $Cr^{+}$ ion is particularly stable, less energy is required to form $Cr^{+}$ , i.e.

$\Delta_{i}H_{1}(Cr)<\Delta_{i}H_{1}(Mn)$

Thus,

Correct order for first ionisation enthalpy:

$\Delta_{i}H_{1}:Mn>Cr$

(Corresponds to option C.)

Second ionisation enthalpy, $\Delta_{i}H_{2}$

Now, let us remove the second electron.

  • Cr:

    From the already stable $Cr^{+}$ ( $[Ar]3d^{5}$ ):

    $Cr^{+} \rightarrow Cr^{2+}+e^{-}$

    After this, $Cr^{2+}$ becomes:

    $[Ar]3d^{4}$ — less stable.

    Therefore, it requires a large amount of energy to remove this second electron.

  • Mn:

    From $Mn^{+}$ ( $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}$ ):

    $Mn^{+} \rightarrow Mn^{2+}+e^{-}$

    After this, $Mn^{2+}$ becomes:

    $[Ar]3d^{5}$ — a stable half-filled configuration.

    Thus, less energy is needed for the second ionisation.

Hence,

$\Delta_{i}H_{2}(Cr)>\Delta_{i}H_{2}(Mn)$

which corresponds to option B.

questions.explanation_html:
For a positive borax bead test, the ion must generally have unpaired electrons in its $d$ -orbitals, because transition metal ions give characteristic bead colours due to electronic transitions.

Let us check each ion:

  • $Fe^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{6}$ → has unpaired electrons, so it gives borax bead test.

  • $Fe^{3+}:[Ar]3d^{5}$ → has unpaired electrons, so it gives borax bead test.

  • $Cr^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{4}$ → has unpaired electrons, so it gives borax bead test.

  • $Zn^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{10}$ → all electrons are paired, so it does not give a positive borax bead test.

So, among the given ions, we compare $Fe^{2+},Fe^{3+},Cr^{2+}$ for highest ionisation enthalpy.

Now, higher positive charge and greater effective nuclear charge generally mean higher ionisation enthalpy. Also, $Fe^{3+}$ has the stable half-filled configuration:

$Fe^{3+}=[Ar]3d^{5}$

This makes removal of another electron more difficult.

Therefore, the ion that:

  • shows positive borax bead test, and

  • has highest ionisation enthalpy

is

$Fe^{3+}$

So, the correct option is D. $Fe^{3+}$ .

questions.explanation_html:
In $MnO_{4}^{2-}$ (manganate ion), oxidation state of Mn is:

$x+4(-2)=-2 \Rightarrow x-8=-2 \Rightarrow x=+6$

In acidic medium, it disproportionates, i.e., Mn in $+6$ state is converted into a higher and a lower oxidation state:

  • Oxidation: $+6 \rightarrow +7$ gives $MnO_{4}^{-}$ (permanganate)

  • Reduction: $+6 \rightarrow +4$ gives $MnO_{2}$

Balanced equation in acidic medium:

$3MnO_{4}^{2-}+4H^{+} \rightarrow 2MnO_{4}^{-}+MnO_{2}+2H_{2}O$

So, $MnO_{4}^{2-}$ disproportionates to $MnO_{4}^{-}$ and $MnO_{2}$ .

Correct option: B

questions.explanation_text: Statement A: Basic vanadium oxide is used in the manufacture of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ . The manufacture of sulphuric acid ( $H_{2}SO_{4}$ ) by the Contact Process is a very important reaction. In this process, the key step is the catalytic oxidation of $SO_{2}$ to $SO_{3}$ : $2SO_{2}(g)+O_{2}(g)\overset{V_{2}O_{5}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}2SO_{3}(g)$ The catalyst used here is Vanadium pentoxide, $V_{2}O_{5}$ . Now, we need to check the nature of this oxide. Let's find the oxidation state of Vanadium (V) in $V_{2}O_{5}$ . Let the oxidation state of V be $x$ . $2(x)+5(-2)=0$ $2x-10=0$ $x=+5$ As a general rule from the d-block elements chapter, metal oxides in higher oxidation states are acidic or amphoteric in nature. Since Vanadium is in its highest oxidation state (+5), $V_{2}O_{5}$ is amphoteric, meaning it reacts with both acids and bases. It is not a basic oxide. So, statement A is incorrect . Statement B: The spin-only magnetic moment value of the transition metal halide employed in Ziegler-Natta polymerization is 2.84 BM. Ziegler-Natta catalysts are used for the polymerization of alkenes, like converting ethene to polyethene. A typical Ziegler-Natta catalyst is a mixture of titanium tetrachloride ( $TiCl_{4}$ ) and triethylaluminium ( $Al(C_{2}H_{5})_{3}$ ). The transition metal halide here is $TiCl_{4}$ . Let's find the magnetic moment for the metal ion in this compound. In $TiCl_{4}$ , the oxidation state of Titanium (Ti) is +4. The atomic number of Ti is 22. Its electronic configuration is $[Ar]3d^{2}4s^{2}$ . The electronic configuration of the $Ti^{4+}$ ion is $[Ar]3d^{0}$ . The number of unpaired electrons ( $n$ ) is 0. The spin-only magnetic moment ( $\mu$ ) is calculated using the formula: $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{B.M.}$ For $Ti^{4+}$ , since $n=0$ , $\mu=\sqrt{0(0+2)}=0\text{B.M.}$ The value given in the statement is 2.84 B.M. A value of $\mu \approx 2.84$ B.M. corresponds to 2 unpaired electrons ( $n=2$ ), because $\sqrt{2(2+2)}=\sqrt{8} \approx 2.83$ B.M. Since the magnetic moment of Ti in $TiCl_{4}$ is 0 B.M., this statement does not hold for the common example of a Ziegler-Natta catalyst. So, statement B is incorrect . Statement C: The p-block metal compound employed in Ziegler-Natta polymerization has the metal in +3 oxidation state. As we just discussed, the Ziegler-Natta catalyst contains a compound like triethylaluminium, $Al(C_{2}H_{5})_{3}$ . Aluminium (Al) belongs to Group 13, which is in the p-block of the periodic table. Let's find the oxidation state of Al in $Al(C_{2}H_{5})_{3}$ . The ethyl group ( $C_{2}H_{5}$ ) is an alkyl group and carries a charge of -1 when bonded to a metal. Let the oxidation state of Al be $x$ . $x+3(-1)=0$ $x=+3$ So, the p-block metal (Al) is indeed in the +3 oxidation state. Therefore, statement C is correct . Statement D: The number of electrons present in the outer most 'd' orbital of metal halide employed in Wacker process is 8. The Wacker process is used for the oxidation of ethene to ethanal (acetaldehyde) using a catalyst. The catalyst used is Palladium(II) chloride, $PdCl_{2}$ , in an aqueous medium. The metal halide here is $PdCl_{2}$ . In $PdCl_{2}$ , the oxidation state of Palladium (Pd) is +2. Palladium (Pd) has atomic number 46. Its electronic configuration is $[Kr]4d^{10}5s^{0}$ . To get the configuration of the $Pd^{2+}$ ion, we remove two electrons. The configuration becomes $[Kr]4d^{8}$ . The outermost 'd' orbital for Palladium is the 4d orbital. The number of electrons in this 4d orbital is 8. Therefore, statement D is correct . Conclusion: We found that statements C and D are correct, while A and B are incorrect. Looking at the options, we need to choose the one that says "C and D Only". The correct answer is Option C .

questions.explanation_text: In acidic medium, $K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}$ acts as a strong oxidising agent. Its orange colour is due to $Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}$ , which gets reduced to green $Cr^{3+}$ : $Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}+14H^{+}+6e^{-} \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+}+7H_{2}O$ So, the species that will change the orange colour must be reducing agents , because they will reduce dichromate to $Cr^{3+}$ . Now check each option. Option A: $Fe^{2+},Sn^{2+},I^{-},S^{2-}$ $Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+}$ : reducing agent $Sn^{2+} \rightarrow Sn^{4+}$ : reducing agent $I^{-} \rightarrow I_{2}$ : reducing agent $S^{2-}$ : strong reducing agent All these can reduce acidified dichromate, so all will change the orange colour. Option B: $S^{2-},Fe^{3+},I^{-},C_{2}O_{4}^{2-}$ $S^{2-}$ : reducing agent $Fe^{3+}$ : not a reducing agent here $I^{-}$ : reducing agent $C_{2}O_{4}^{2-}$ : reducing agent Since $Fe^{3+}$ will not reduce dichromate, this option is incorrect. Option C: $Fe^{2+},NO_{2}^{-},SO_{2},Sn^{4+}$ $Fe^{2+}$ : reducing agent $NO_{2}^{-}$ : can act as reducing agent $SO_{2}$ : reducing agent $Sn^{4+}$ : already in higher oxidation state, not a reducing agent So this option is incorrect. Option D: $Fe^{3+},SO_{4}^{2-},S^{2-},Sn^{4+}$ $Fe^{3+}$ : not reducing $SO_{4}^{2-}$ : not reducing $S^{2-}$ : reducing $Sn^{4+}$ : not reducing So this is also incorrect. Therefore, the correct answer is: $\text{Option A}$

In acidic medium, $K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}$ acts as a strong oxidising agent.

Its orange colour is due to $Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}$ , which gets reduced to green $Cr^{3+}$ :

$Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}+14H^{+}+6e^{-} \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+}+7H_{2}O$

So, the species that will change the orange colour must be reducing agents, because they will reduce dichromate to $Cr^{3+}$ .

Now check each option.

Option A: $Fe^{2+},Sn^{2+},I^{-},S^{2-}$

  • $Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+}$ : reducing agent

  • $Sn^{2+} \rightarrow Sn^{4+}$ : reducing agent

  • $I^{-} \rightarrow I_{2}$ : reducing agent

  • $S^{2-}$ : strong reducing agent

All these can reduce acidified dichromate, so all will change the orange colour.

Option B: $S^{2-},Fe^{3+},I^{-},C_{2}O_{4}^{2-}$

  • $S^{2-}$ : reducing agent

  • $Fe^{3+}$ : not a reducing agent here

  • $I^{-}$ : reducing agent

  • $C_{2}O_{4}^{2-}$ : reducing agent

Since $Fe^{3+}$ will not reduce dichromate, this option is incorrect.

Option C: $Fe^{2+},NO_{2}^{-},SO_{2},Sn^{4+}$

  • $Fe^{2+}$ : reducing agent

  • $NO_{2}^{-}$ : can act as reducing agent

  • $SO_{2}$ : reducing agent

  • $Sn^{4+}$ : already in higher oxidation state, not a reducing agent

So this option is incorrect.

Option D: $Fe^{3+},SO_{4}^{2-},S^{2-},Sn^{4+}$

  • $Fe^{3+}$ : not reducing

  • $SO_{4}^{2-}$ : not reducing

  • $S^{2-}$ : reducing

  • $Sn^{4+}$ : not reducing

So this is also incorrect.

Therefore, the correct answer is:

$\text{Option A}$

questions.explanation_text: First, write the electronic configurations of Cr and Mn. $\begin{aligned} & Cr=(Ar)3d^{5}4s^{1} \\ & Mn=(Ar)3d^{5}4s^{2} \\ & IE_{1}(Cr)<IE_{1}(Mn) \\ & IE_{2}(Cr)>IE_{2}(Mn) \\ & IE_{3}(Cr)<IE_{3}(Mn) \end{aligned}$ For first ionization enthalpy ( $IE_{1}$ ): In Cr, the electron is removed from $4s^{1}$ . After losing this one $4s$ electron, Cr becomes $Cr^{+}$ with a stable half-filled $3d^{5}$ configuration. So removing the first electron is comparatively easier, hence $IE_{1}(Cr)<IE_{1}(Mn)$ . For second ionization enthalpy ( $IE_{2}$ ): After losing one electron, $Cr^{+}$ already has the stable $3d^{5}$ configuration. Removing the second electron would disturb this stable half-filled $3d$ arrangement, so it needs more energy. But in Mn, after the first electron loss, removing the next electron can lead to $Mn^{2+}$ with stable $3d^{5}$ . Therefore, $IE_{2}(Cr)>IE_{2}(Mn)$ . For third ionization enthalpy ( $IE_{3}$ ): $Mn^{2+}$ is very stable due to $3d^{5}$ . Removing one more electron from this stable state is difficult, so $IE_{3}$ for Mn becomes high. In comparison, $Cr^{2+}$ does not have this extra stability, so removing the third electron is relatively easier. Hence, $IE_{3}(Cr)<IE_{3}(Mn)$ .

$Re,Os_{s}$

The higher melting point of $Re$ is due to the strength of atomic bonding.

Osmium tills weaker metallic bonds than $Re$ due to its crystal arrangement and electronic Structure.

Comparing Re, and OS,

$R_{e}$ is slightly smaller in atomic radius which allows atoms to pack more efficiently than is and has stronger bonds and higher meeting point.

So,

$\begin{aligned} & M_{n}<Fe \\ & T_{c}<Ru \\ & O_{s}<Re \end{aligned}$

Option 4) $Mn<Fe,TC<Ru$ and $Os<Re$ .

questions.question_html: Niobium $(Nb)$ and ruthenium $(Ru)$ have " $x$ " and " $y$ " number of electrons in their respective 4 d orbitals. The value of $x+y$ is __________.
questions.explanation_text: We need to determine the number of electrons each element has in its 4d orbitals and then add them together. 1. Niobium $(Nb,Z=41)$ The ground‐state electronic configuration of niobium is: $[Kr]4d^{4}5s^{1}.$ Hence, Niobium has 4 electrons in its 4d orbitals . 2. Ruthenium $(Ru,Z=44)$ The ground‐state electronic configuration of ruthenium is: $[Kr]4d^{7}5s^{1}.$ Hence, Ruthenium has 7 electrons in its 4d orbitals . 3. Sum of 4d Electrons $x=4(\text{for Nb}),y=7(\text{for Ru}).$ Therefore, $x+y=4+7=11.$ Answer: 11
questions.explanation_html:
We need to determine the number of electrons each element has in its 4d orbitals and then add them together.

1. Niobium $(Nb,Z=41)$

The ground‐state electronic configuration of niobium is:

$[Kr]4d^{4}5s^{1}.$

Hence, Niobium has 4 electrons in its 4d orbitals.

2. Ruthenium $(Ru,Z=44)$

The ground‐state electronic configuration of ruthenium is:

$[Kr]4d^{7}5s^{1}.$

Hence, Ruthenium has 7 electrons in its 4d orbitals.

3. Sum of 4d Electrons

$x=4(\text{for Nb}),y=7(\text{for Ru}).$

Therefore,

$x+y=4+7=11.$

Answer: 11

questions.explanation_text: Let's analyze the electron configurations of the given lanthanide ions. Europium ( $Eu$ ) The neutral atom of Eu (atomic number 63) typically has the configuration: $[Xe]4f^{7}6s^{2}.$ For $Eu^{2+}$ , two electrons are removed, usually from the $6s$ orbital, resulting in: $[Xe]4f^{7}.$ Thus, $Eu^{2+}$ has a $4f^{7}$ configuration. For $Eu^{3+}$ , three electrons are removed (the two $6s$ electrons and one $4f$ electron), giving: $[Xe]4f^{6}.$ Therefore, $Eu^{3+}$ does not have a $4f^{7}$ configuration. Gadolinium ( $Gd$ ) The neutral atom of Gd (atomic number 64) is usually represented as: $[Xe]4f^{7}5d^{1}6s^{2}.$ For $Gd^{3+}$ , three electrons are removed (typically the $5d^{1}$ and the two $6s$ electrons), resulting in: $[Xe]4f^{7}.$ So, $Gd^{3+}$ has a $4f^{7}$ configuration. Terbium ( $Tb$ ) The neutral atom of Tb (atomic number 65) typically has the configuration: $[Xe]4f^{9}6s^{2}.$ For $Tb^{3+}$ , removal of three electrons gives: $[Xe]4f^{8}.$ Hence, $Tb^{3+}$ does not have a $4f^{7}$ configuration. Samarium ( $Sm$ ) The neutral atom of Sm (atomic number 62) generally has: $[Xe]4f^{6}6s^{2}.$ For $Sm^{2+}$ , after removal of two electrons (likely from the $6s$ orbital), the configuration is: $[Xe]4f^{6}.$ Therefore, $Sm^{2+}$ does not have a $4f^{7}$ configuration. Thus, the ions with a $4f^{7}$ configuration are: (A) $Eu^{2+}$ (B) $Gd^{3+}$ The correct answer is: Option D – (A) and (B) only.

questions.question_html:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A) : In aqueous solutions $Cr^{2+}$ is reducing while $Mn^{3+}$ is oxidising in nature.

Reason (R) : Extra stability to half filled electronic configuration is observed than incompletely filled electronic configuration.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

options.label: A
options.html: (A) is true but (R) is false

options.label: B

options.html: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

questions.explanation_text: Let us analyze both the Assertion (A) and the Reason (R) to determine the correct answer. Assertion (A) : In aqueous solutions, $Cr^{2+}$ is reducing while $Mn^{3+}$ is oxidising in nature. This assertion is true. The $Cr^{2+}$ ion has a tendency to be oxidized to $Cr^{3+}$ because $Cr^{3+}$ has a more stable electronic configuration. Therefore, $Cr^{2+}$ acts as a reducing agent. On the other hand, $Mn^{3+}$ tends to stabilize by being reduced to $Mn^{2+}$ , which is a more stable electronic configuration due to having a half-filled d5 subshell ( $Mn^{2+}$ : [Ar] 3d 5 ). Thus, $Mn^{3+}$ acts as an oxidizing agent. Reason (R) : Extra stability to half filled electronic configuration is observed than incompletely filled electronic configuration. This reason is also true. Half-filled and fully filled electron configurations, like those found in $Mn^{2+}$ and $Cr^{0}$ respectively, are particularly stable due to symmetry and exchange energy considerations. This is a reason why certain ions like $Mn^{3+}$ want to be reduced to $Mn^{2+}$ , and why $Cr^{0}$ (with a [Ar] 3d 5 4s 1 configuration) is not as common as $Cr^{3+}$ (which has a [Ar] 3d 3 configuration, and while not half-filled, is favored due to crystal field stabilization energy considerations in octahedral complexes). If we evaluate these statements together, we see that Assertion (A) is directly related to the electronic configurations and their stability, as asserted by Reason (R). The stability of half-filled and full orbitals contributes to the observed redox behavior of $Cr^{2+}$ and $Mn^{3+}$ in aqueous solutions. Therefore, the correct answer is Option B : Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

questions.explanation_text: The magnetic moment of an atom or ion with unpaired electrons is given by the formula $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$ Bohr magnetons (BM), where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons. The magnetic moment depends on the number of unpaired electrons: more unpaired electrons lead to a higher magnetic moment. Looking at the given options with respect to their electron configurations and calculating their respective magnetic moments based on their unpaired electrons: $[Ar]3d^{7}$ has 3 unpaired electrons, yielding a magnetic moment of $\sqrt{15}$ BM. $[Ar]3d^{8}$ has 2 unpaired electrons, for a magnetic moment of $\sqrt{8}$ BM. $[Ar]3d^{3}$ also has 3 unpaired electrons, similar to $3d^{7}$ , so its magnetic moment is likewise $\sqrt{15}$ BM. Finally, $[Ar]3d^{6}$ has 4 unpaired electrons, resulting in the highest magnetic moment among the options, $\sqrt{24}$ BM. Hence, the electron configuration associated with the highest magnetic moment is $[Ar]3d^{6}$ .

questions.question_text: Among $CrO,Cr_{2}O_{3}$ and $CrO_{3}$ , the sum of spin-only magnetic moment values of basic and amphoteric oxides is _________ $10^{-2}BM$ (nearest integer). (Given atomic number of $Cr$ is 24 )
questions.question_html:
Among $CrO,Cr_{2}O_{3}$ and $CrO_{3}$ , the sum of spin-only magnetic moment values of basic and amphoteric oxides is _________ $10^{-2}BM$ (nearest integer).

(Given atomic number of $Cr$ is 24 )
questions.explanation_text: First, we need to understand the oxidation states of chromium in the given compounds and determine their magnetic moments based on their electronic configurations. 1. $CrO$ : In $CrO$ , the oxidation state of chromium is +2. The electronic configuration of chromium (Cr) is $1s^{2}2s^{2}2p^{6}3s^{2}3p^{6}3d^{5}4s^{1}$ . In the +2 oxidation state, two electrons are removed, typically from the 4s and one of the 3d orbitals, leaving us with the configuration $3d^{4}$ . To find the spin-only magnetic moment, we use the formula: $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}BM$ where n is the number of unpaired electrons. For $Cr^{2+}$ , we have 4 unpaired electrons in the 3d orbitals. Thus, $\mu=\sqrt{4(4+2)}=\sqrt{24} \approx 4.90BM$ 2. $Cr_{2}O_{3}$ : In $Cr_{2}O_{3}$ , the oxidation state of chromium is +3. The electronic configuration of $Cr^{3+}$ is $3d^{3}$ after losing three electrons. For $Cr^{3+}$ , there are 3 unpaired electrons. Thus, $\mu=\sqrt{3(3+2)}=\sqrt{15} \approx 3.87BM$ 3. $CrO_{3}$ : In $CrO_{3}$ , the oxidation state of chromium is +6. The electronic configuration of $Cr^{6+}$ is $3d^{0}$ after losing six electrons. There are no unpaired electrons for $Cr^{6+}$ . Since $Cr^{6+}$ has no unpaired electrons, its spin-only magnetic moment is 0 BM. The magnetic moment values for each compound are: $CrO$ : 4.90 BM (basic oxide) $Cr_{2}O_{3}$ : 3.87 BM (amphoteric oxide) $CrO_{3}$ : 0 BM The sum of the spin-only magnetic moments of the basic and amphoteric oxides is: $4.90+3.87=8.77BM$ Expressing in terms of $10^{-2}BM$ , $8.77BM \times 100=877( \times 10^{-2}BM)$ Thus, the sum of spin-only magnetic moment values of basic and amphoteric oxides is approximately 877 $\times 10^{-2}BM$ (nearest integer).

In the +2 oxidation state, two electrons are removed, typically from the 4s and one of the 3d orbitals, leaving us with the configuration $3d^{4}$ .

To find the spin-only magnetic moment, we use the formula:

$\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}BM$

where n is the number of unpaired electrons. For $Cr^{2+}$ , we have 4 unpaired electrons in the 3d orbitals.

2. $Cr_{2}O_{3}$ : In $Cr_{2}O_{3}$ , the oxidation state of chromium is +3. The electronic configuration of $Cr^{3+}$ is $3d^{3}$ after losing three electrons.

Any metal ion with a negative standard reduction potential compared to hydrogen has the ability to liberate hydrogen gas from dilute acids because they are more likely to donate electrons to the $H^{+}$ ions found in acids, reducing them to $H_{2}$ gas. The standard reduction potentials for the ions mentioned are as follows: $Ti^{2+}/Ti$ is more negative than that of $H^{+}/H_{2}$ . $Cr^{2+}/Cr$ also has a more negative standard reduction potential compared to $H^{+}/H_{2}$ . questions.question_text: A transition metal ' $M$ ' among $Sc,Ti,V,Cr,Mn$ and $Fe$ has the highest second ionisation enthalpy. The spin-only magnetic moment value of $M^{+}$ ion is _______ BM (Near integer) (Given atomic number $Sc:21,Ti:22,V:23,Cr:24,Mn:25,Fe:26$ )
questions.question_html:
A transition metal ' $M$ ' among $Sc,Ti,V,Cr,Mn$ and $Fe$ has the highest second ionisation enthalpy. The spin-only magnetic moment value of $M^{+}$ ion is _______ BM (Near integer)

(Given atomic number $Sc:21,Ti:22,V:23,Cr:24,Mn:25,Fe:26$ )
questions.explanation_text: Identify which metal (M) has the highest second ionization enthalpy. We are comparing the elements Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, and Fe in terms of their second ionization enthalpy (IE₂). Recall: The second ionization enthalpy (IE₂) is the energy required to remove one electron from the singly charged ion $M^{+}$ to form $M^{2+}$ . For most 3d transition metals, the first electron is removed from the 4s orbital. Particularly large values of IE₂ often occur if, after removal of the first electron, one is forced to remove an electron from a stable configuration (e.g., half-filled d-orbital). Let us outline the ground-state (neutral atom) electron configurations and the removal of the first and second electrons: Sc $[Ar]3d^{1}4s^{2}$ $Sc \rightarrow Sc^{+}$ : remove 1 electron from 4s $Sc^{+} \rightarrow Sc^{2+}$ : remove the second 4s electron Final: $Sc^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{1}$ Ti $[Ar]3d^{2}4s^{2}$ 1st electron from 4s → $Ti^{+}=[Ar]3d^{2}4s^{1}$ 2nd electron from 4s → $Ti^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{2}$ V $[Ar]3d^{3}4s^{2}$ 1st electron from 4s → $V^{+}=[Ar]3d^{3}4s^{1}$ 2nd electron from 4s → $V^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{3}$ Cr $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}$ 1st electron from 4s → $Cr^{+}=[Ar]3d^{5}$ (a stable half-filled d $^{5}$ configuration) 2nd electron now must come from the 3d shell → $Cr^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{4}$ Because removing an electron from a half-filled d $^{5}$ orbital costs a lot of energy, $Cr$ generally has a notably high second IE. Mn $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{2}$ 1st electron from 4s → $Mn^{+}=[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}$ 2nd electron from 4s → $Mn^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{5}$ (thus still d $^{5}$ in the end) The second ionization for Mn is large but less dramatic than for Cr because Mn $^{2+}$ ends with a half-filled d $^{5}$ . You are not removing from a half-filled d $^{5}$ to get Mn $^{2+}$ . Fe $[Ar]3d^{6}4s^{2}$ 1st electron from 4s → $Fe^{+}=[Ar]3d^{6}4s^{1}$ 2nd electron from 4s → $Fe^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{6}$ From experimental data (and the arguments above), $Cr$ indeed has the highest second ionization enthalpy among these six metals. Determine the electronic configuration of $Cr^{+}$ and its spin-only magnetic moment. Neutral $Cr$ : $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}$ $Cr^{+}$ : Removal of the 4s electron ⇒ $[Ar]3d^{5}$ The $3d^{5}$ configuration has 5 unpaired electrons . The spin-only magnetic moment $\mu$ is given by $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}BM,$ where $n$ = number of unpaired electrons. Here $n=5$ , so $\mu=\sqrt{5(5+2)}=\sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\text{BM}.$ This is often rounded to about 5.9 or 6.0 BM .
questions.explanation_html:
Identify which metal (M) has the highest second ionization enthalpy.

We are comparing the elements Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, and Fe in terms of their second ionization enthalpy (IE₂). Recall:

The second ionization enthalpy (IE₂) is the energy required to remove one electron from the singly charged ion $M^{+}$ to form $M^{2+}$ .

For most 3d transition metals, the first electron is removed from the 4s orbital.

Particularly large values of IE₂ often occur if, after removal of the first electron, one is forced to remove an electron from a stable configuration (e.g., half-filled d-orbital).

Let us outline the ground-state (neutral atom) electron configurations and the removal of the first and second electrons:

Sc $[Ar]3d^{1}4s^{2}$

$Sc \rightarrow Sc^{+}$ : remove 1 electron from 4s

$Sc^{+} \rightarrow Sc^{2+}$ : remove the second 4s electron

Final: $Sc^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{1}$

Ti $[Ar]3d^{2}4s^{2}$

1st electron from 4s → $Ti^{+}=[Ar]3d^{2}4s^{1}$

2nd electron from 4s → $Ti^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{2}$

V $[Ar]3d^{3}4s^{2}$

1st electron from 4s → $V^{+}=[Ar]3d^{3}4s^{1}$

2nd electron from 4s → $V^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{3}$

Cr $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}$

1st electron from 4s → $Cr^{+}=[Ar]3d^{5}$ (a stable half-filled d $^{5}$ configuration)

2nd electron now must come from the 3d shell → $Cr^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{4}$

Because removing an electron from a half-filled d $^{5}$ orbital costs a lot of energy, $Cr$ generally has a notably high second IE.

Mn $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{2}$

1st electron from 4s → $Mn^{+}=[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}$

2nd electron from 4s → $Mn^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{5}$ (thus still d $^{5}$ in the end)

The second ionization for Mn is large but less dramatic than for Cr because Mn $^{2+}$ ends with a half-filled d $^{5}$ . You are not removing from a half-filled d $^{5}$ to get Mn $^{2+}$ .

Fe $[Ar]3d^{6}4s^{2}$

1st electron from 4s → $Fe^{+}=[Ar]3d^{6}4s^{1}$

2nd electron from 4s → $Fe^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{6}$

From experimental data (and the arguments above), $Cr$ indeed has the highest second ionization enthalpy among these six metals.

Determine the electronic configuration of $Cr^{+}$ and its spin-only magnetic moment.

Neutral $Cr$ : $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}$

$Cr^{+}$ : Removal of the 4s electron ⇒ $[Ar]3d^{5}$

The $3d^{5}$ configuration has 5 unpaired electrons.

The spin-only magnetic moment $\mu$ is given by

$\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}BM,$

where $n$ = number of unpaired electrons. Here $n=5$ , so

$\mu=\sqrt{5(5+2)}=\sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\text{BM}.$

This is often rounded to about 5.9 or 6.0 BM.

questions.explanation_text: To determine the spin-only magnetic moments of products A and B formed from the fusion of chromite ore with sodium carbonate in the presence of air, we first need to examine the given reaction and the properties of the products. The reaction provided is: $4FeCr_{2}O_{4}+8Na_{2}CO_{3}+7O_{2} \rightarrow 8Na_{2}CrO_{4}(A)+2Fe_{2}O_{3}(B)+8CO_{2}$ Identifying the Products: Product A is sodium chromate, $Na_{2}CrO_{4}$ . Product B is ferric oxide, $Fe_{2}O_{3}$ . Determining the Magnetic Moments: For Product A ( $Na_{2}CrO_{4}$ ): In $Na_{2}CrO_{4}$ , the chromium is in the +6 oxidation state. The electronic configuration of $Cr^{6+}$ is $[Ar]3d^{0}$ . Since there are no unpaired electrons in the $3d$ orbitals, the spin-only magnetic moment is zero. $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{BM}=\sqrt{0(0+2)}\text{BM}=0\text{BM}$ For Product B ( $Fe_{2}O_{3}$ ): In $Fe_{2}O_{3}$ , the iron is in the +3 oxidation state. The electronic configuration of $Fe^{3+}$ is $[Ar]3d^{5}$ . $Fe^{3+}$ has 5 unpaired electrons in the $3d$ orbitals. The spin-only magnetic moment can be calculated using the formula: $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{BM}=\sqrt{5(5+2)}\text{BM}=\sqrt{35}\text{BM} \approx 5.9\text{BM}$ Sum of Magnetic Moments: The spin-only magnetic moment of Product A is $0\text{BM}$ . The spin-only magnetic moment of Product B is $5.9\text{BM}$ . Therefore, the sum of the spin-only magnetic moments of A and B is: $0+5.9 \approx 6\text{BM}$ Conclusion: The sum of the spin-only magnetic moment values of A and B is approximately 6 B.M. (to the nearest integer).

questions.question_html:
Total number of ions from the following with noble gas configuration is _________.

$Sr^{2+}(z=38),Cs^{+}(z=55),La^{2+}(z=57),Pb^{2+}(z=82),Yb^{2+}(z=70)$ and $Fe^{2+}(z=26)$
questions.explanation_text: To determine which of these ions have a noble gas configuration, we must consider what the phrase "noble gas configuration" means. Atoms or ions with a noble gas configuration have completely filled electron shells, similar to the electron configuration of the noble gases, which are the elements found in Group 18 of the periodic table. Noble gases are helium (He), neon (Ne), argon (Ar), krypton (Kr), xenon (Xe), and radon (Rn). Let's examine each ion given: $Sr^{2+}(z=38)$ : Strontium has atomic number 38 and loses 2 electrons to form a $Sr^{2+}$ ion, giving it the same electron configuration as krypton (Kr), with atomic number 36. Hence, it has a noble gas configuration. $[Sr^{2+}]=[Kr]$ $Cs^{+}(z=55)$ : Cesium has atomic number 55, and by losing 1 electron to form $Cs^{+}$ , it has the electron configuration of xenon (Xe), with atomic number 54. Thus, it also has a noble gas configuration. $[Cs^{+}]=[Xe]$ $La^{2+}(z=57)$ : Lanthanum has atomic number 57. If it lost 2 electrons to form $La^{2+}$ , it would not have a noble gas configuration because it would have one electron more than xenon (Xe), which means it would not fully match any noble gas electron configuration. $[La^{2+}]=[Xe]5d^{1}$ $Pb^{2+}(z=82)$ : Lead has an atomic number of 82, so when it loses 2 electrons to form $Pb^{2+}$ , it has 80 electrons, which is the same electron number as mercury (Hg) and not a noble gas. Therefore, $Pb^{2+}$ does not have a noble gas configuration. $[Pb^{2+}]=[Xe]4f^{14}5d^{10}6s^{2}$ $Yb^{2+}(z=70)$ : Ytterbium has an atomic number of 70. By losing 2 electrons to form $Yb^{2+}$ , it has 68 electrons, aligning with the electron configuration of Erbium (Er). $Yb^{2+}$ and not a noble gas. $[Yb^{2+}]=[Xe]4f^{14}$ $Fe^{2+}(z=26)$ : Iron has an atomic number of 26. When it becomes $Fe^{2+}$ by losing 2 electrons, it has 24 electrons. This does not correspond to any noble gas configuration, as the nearest noble gas is argon (Ar) with 18 electrons. $[Fe^{2+}]=[Ar]3d^{6}$ Therefore, the ions $Sr^{2+}$ and $Cs^{+}$ have a noble gas configuration. Altogether, there are 2 ions with a noble gas configuration.

questions.question_html:
The electronic configuration of Einsteinium is :

questions.explanation_text: The correct option for the electronic configuration of Einsteinium (atomic number 99) is: Option C: [Rn] 5f 11 6d 0 7s 2 Here's why: Atomic Number and Electrons: Einsteinium has an atomic number of 99, which means it has 99 protons in its nucleus. Since atoms are neutral, it also has 99 electrons surrounding the nucleus. Electron Shells: Electrons fill up energy shells around the nucleus. The order of filling follows the Aufbau principle, which generally fills lower energy shells before moving to higher ones. Noble Gas Core Notation: The notation [Rn] represents the filled electron configuration of Radon (atomic number 86). This is a shorthand to avoid writing out the entire configuration of the inner shells, as they are not involved in the chemical behavior of Einsteinium. Filling the f-orbital: Einsteinium is an actinide element, located in the f-block of the periodic table. The 5f subshell fills up after the 6s subshell. Aufbau Principle: According to the Aufbau principle, the 5f subshell can hold up to 14 electrons. In Einsteinium, 11 electrons fill the 5f subshell (5f 11 ). Empty d-orbital: The 6d subshell has a higher energy level than the 5f subshell. Since the 5f subshell isn't completely filled, the 6d subshell remains empty (6d 0 ). Outermost Electrons: The remaining two electrons fill the outermost 7s subshell (7s 2 ). Therefore, the complete electronic configuration of Einsteinium is: [Rn] 5f 11 6d 0 7s 2
questions.explanation_html:
The correct option for the electronic configuration of Einsteinium (atomic number 99) is:

Option C: [Rn] 5f11 6d0 7s2

Here's why:

  1. Atomic Number and Electrons: Einsteinium has an atomic number of 99, which means it has 99 protons in its nucleus. Since atoms are neutral, it also has 99 electrons surrounding the nucleus.

  2. Electron Shells: Electrons fill up energy shells around the nucleus. The order of filling follows the Aufbau principle, which generally fills lower energy shells before moving to higher ones.

  3. Noble Gas Core Notation: The notation [Rn] represents the filled electron configuration of Radon (atomic number 86). This is a shorthand to avoid writing out the entire configuration of the inner shells, as they are not involved in the chemical behavior of Einsteinium.

  4. Filling the f-orbital: Einsteinium is an actinide element, located in the f-block of the periodic table. The 5f subshell fills up after the 6s subshell.

  5. Aufbau Principle: According to the Aufbau principle, the 5f subshell can hold up to 14 electrons. In Einsteinium, 11 electrons fill the 5f subshell (5f11).

  6. Empty d-orbital: The 6d subshell has a higher energy level than the 5f subshell. Since the 5f subshell isn't completely filled, the 6d subshell remains empty (6d0).

  7. Outermost Electrons: The remaining two electrons fill the outermost 7s subshell (7s2).

Therefore, the complete electronic configuration of Einsteinium is:

[Rn] 5f11 6d0 7s2

questions.question_html:
The electronic configuration for Neodymium is:

[Atomic Number for Neodymium 60]
questions.explanation_text: The electronic configuration of an element is determined by adding electrons to atomic orbitals following the Aufbau principle, the Pauli exclusion principle, and Hund's rule. For atoms with atomic numbers higher than that of xenon (Xe, atomic number 54), the electrons start filling the outer orbitals following the xenon core. In this case, we're looking at neodymium (Nd), which has an atomic number of 60. To find the electronic configuration of neodymium, we first note the configuration of xenon, which serves as the core, and then add the additional electrons beyond xenon to the relevant orbitals. Neodymium has 60 - 54 = 6 electrons more than xenon. These additional electrons will fill the 4f and 6s orbitals. Based on its position in the periodic table, neodymium’s electrons start filling the 4f orbitals before the 5d. Since the 6s orbital is at a lower energy level than the 4f orbital, it gets filled before the 4f. Neodymium will have 2 electrons in the 6s orbital, and the remaining 4 electrons will go into the 4f orbital. Therefore, the correct electronic configuration for neodymium is: $[Xe]4f^{4}6s^{2}$ So, Option A is the correct answer.

questions.question_text: Number of colourless lanthanoid ions among the following is __________. $Eu^{3+},Lu^{3+},Nd^{3+},La^{3+},Sm^{3+}$
questions.question_html:
Number of colourless lanthanoid ions among the following is __________.

$Eu^{3+},Lu^{3+},Nd^{3+},La^{3+},Sm^{3+}$
questions.explanation_text: The color of lanthanoid ions in solutions is mainly due to the electronic transitions within the 4f subshell. The lanthanoid ions are more likely to be colorless when they have fully filled (with 14 electrons) or completely empty (with 0 electrons) f orbitals because, in these cases, there are no electrons to undergo f-f transitions, and as a result, no absorption of visible light occurs leading to colorlessness. Let's consider the electronic configurations of the lanthanoid ions provided: - $Eu^{3+}$ : Europium (Eu) has an atomic number of 63. Neutral europium ([Xe]4f 7 6s^2) loses three electrons to form Eu 3+ , leaving it with an electronic configuration equivalent to [Xe]4f 6 . With 6 electrons in the f orbital, it can undergo f-f transitions, thus it is not colorless. - $Lu^{3+}$ : Lutetium (Lu) has an atomic number of 71. In its 3+ ionic state, lutetium has lost its 6s and 5d electrons and is left with a completely filled 4f orbital ([Xe] 4f 14 ). This configuration cannot allow for any f-f transitions, as there are no available energy levels within the f orbital for an electron to jump to, making Lu 3+ colorless. - $Nd^{3+}$ : Neodymium (Nd) has an atomic number of 60. In its 3+ state ([Xe] 4f 3 ), it clearly has partially filled f orbitals, which can absorb visible light for f-f transitions, so it is not colorless. - $La^{3+}$ : Lanthanum (La) has an atomic number of 57. In its 3+ ionic state, it has a configuration of [Xe], meaning that its 4f orbital is completely empty. Since there are no electrons in the f orbital to undergo f-f transitions, La 3+ is colorless. - $Sm^{3+}$ : Samarium (Sm) has an atomic number of 62. As a 3+ ion ([Xe] 4f 5 ), it too has electrons in the f orbital capable of undergoing f-f transitions, so it is not colorless. From the analysis, the colorless lanthanoid ions among the ones listed are $Lu^{3+}$ and $La^{3+}$ . Therefore, the number of colorless lanthanoid ions among the given options is 2 .

questions.explanation_text: To evaluate the given statements, let's analyze each statement in the context of chemical principles: Statement I: The higher oxidation states are more stable down the group among transition elements unlike p-block elements. This statement is true. In transition elements, as we move down the group, the electrons are being added to the n-1 d orbitals, where 'n' represents the principal quantum number. The ability to exhibit higher oxidation states stems from the fact that not only are the s electrons of the outermost shell used in bonding, but the d electrons are also involved. Moreover, down the group, the effective nuclear charge decreases, and the shielding effect increases, so electrons from both s and d orbitals can be easily used for bonding, leading to stable higher oxidation states. This trend is opposite in the case of p-block elements, where the stability of higher oxidation states generally decreases down the group due to the inert pair effect, which makes it hard to remove electrons from the s orbital as we move down the group. Statement II: Copper can not liberate hydrogen from weak acids. This statement is also true. Copper (Cu) is less reactive and lies below hydrogen in the electrochemical series, meaning it has a higher reduction potential than hydrogen. For a metal to displace hydrogen from an acid, it must have a lower reduction potential than hydrogen. This is not the case with copper. Therefore, copper does not react with weak acids (like acetic acid) to liberate hydrogen gas. This behavior can be explained through the electrochemical series, where metals placed above hydrogen are capable of displacing hydrogen from acids (exemplified by metals such as zinc or magnesium), whereas copper does not have this ability due to its relative placement in the series. Based on the analysis, Option C is the correct answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

It does not commonly exhibit other oxidation states because removing more than three electrons would require removing electrons from the very stable noble gas core configuration ([Ar]), which is energetically unfavorable. Therefore, the correct answer is Option D: Scandium .

  • Scandium (Sc), however, primarily exhibits a +3 oxidation state in its compounds (excluding its 0 state in the elemental form). This is because scandium has an electronic configuration of [Ar]3d14s2, and it loses all three outer electrons to achieve a stable configuration, resulting in a +3 oxidation state. It does not commonly exhibit other oxidation states because removing more than three electrons would require removing electrons from the very stable noble gas core configuration ([Ar]), which is energetically unfavorable.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option D: Scandium.

questions.question_text: Among $VO_{2}^{+},MnO_{4}^{-}$ and $Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}$ , the spin-only magnetic moment value of the species with least oxidising ability is __________ BM (Nearest integer). (Given atomic member $V=23,Mn=25,Cr=24$ )
questions.question_html:
Among $VO_{2}^{+},MnO_{4}^{-}$ and $Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}$ , the spin-only magnetic moment value of the species with least oxidising ability is __________ BM (Nearest integer).

(Given atomic member $V=23,Mn=25,Cr=24$ )
questions.explanation_text: In order to determine the spin-only magnetic moment value of the species with the least oxidizing ability, we first need to analyze their oxidation states and electron configurations. 1. $VO_{2}^{+}$ : For vanadium in $VO_{2}^{+}$ , the oxidation state is +5. The electronic configuration of V is $[Ar]3d^{3}4s^{2}$ . Thus, in +5 oxidation state, vanadium will have zero d-electrons (since it loses 5 electrons) and, consequently, $VO_{2}^{+}$ is diamagnetic (since zero unpaired electrons). 2. $MnO_{4}^{-}$ : For manganese in $MnO_{4}^{-}$ , the oxidation state is +7. The electronic configuration of Mn is $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{2}$ . Thus, in +7 oxidation state, manganese will have zero d-electrons (since it loses 7 electrons) and, consequently, $MnO_{4}^{-}$ is also diamagnetic (since zero unpaired electrons). 3. $Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}$ : For chromium in $Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}$ , we have two chromium atoms. Each chromium is in the +6 oxidation state. The electronic configuration of Cr is $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}$ . Thus, in +6 oxidation state, each chromium will have zero d-electrons (since it loses 6 electrons) and, consequently, $Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}$ is also diamagnetic (since zero unpaired electrons). From these observations, we note that all the species we analyzed are diamagnetic. However, to identify the species with the least oxidizing ability, we look at their standard reduction potentials (E° values). Typically, the oxidizing ability increases with increasing positive E° values. Given the nature of these species, we can infer that: $MnO_{4}^{-}$ is a very strong oxidizing agent (very high E° value). $Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}$ is also a strong oxidizing agent (high but less than $MnO_{4}^{-}$ ). $VO_{2}^{+}$ has a moderate oxidizing ability (lesser E° value than both $MnO_{4}^{-}$ and $Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}$ ). Therefore, among the given species, $VO_{2}^{+}$ has the least oxidizing ability. As mentioned previously, $VO_{2}^{+}$ has zero unpaired electrons, making it diamagnetic. The spin-only magnetic moment is given by the formula: $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$ where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons. For $VO_{2}^{+}$ , $n=0$ , thus: $\mu=\sqrt{0(0+2)}=0\text{BM}$ Given the options, the nearest integer value of the spin-only magnetic moment for the species with the least oxidizing ability (which is $VO_{2}^{+}$ ) is indeed: 0 BM

questions.explanation_text: Potassium permanganate ( $KMnO_{4}$ ) is a strong oxidizing agent that can oxidize iodide ions ( $I^{-}$ ) to different products depending on the pH of the solution. In acidic solutions, $KMnO_{4}$ oxidizes $I^{-}$ to molecular iodine ( $I_{2}$ ) according to the following equation: $2MnO_{4}^{-}+16H^{+}+10I^{-} \rightarrow 2Mn^{2+}+8H_{2}O+5I_{2}$ In neutral or faintly alkaline solutions, the oxidation product is different because the $I^{-}$ is oxidized to iodate ion ( $IO_{3}^{-}$ ). The reaction in a neutral or slightly alkaline solution is as follows: $2MnO_{4}^{-}+2H_{2}O+10I^{-} \rightarrow 2MnO_{2}+4OH^{-}+5IO_{3}^{-}$ So according to the reactions above, in acidic solutions, $I^{-}$ is oxidized to $I_{2}$ while in neutral or faintly alkaline solutions, $I^{-}$ is oxidized to $IO_{3}^{-}$ . Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C: $I_{2}&IO_{3}^{-}$

Ferrous ammonium sulfate is not broken apart by heat, so prolonged heating is not necessary to prevent breaking. Option D: Reduction is the process of a chemical compound gaining electrons. Reason R : Low oxidation states are found when a complex has ligands capable of $\pi$ -donor character in addition to the $\sigma$ -bonding. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
questions.question_html:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as "Assertion A" and the other is labelled as "Reason R"

Assertion A : In the complex $Ni(CO)_{4}$ and $Fe(CO)_{5}$ , the metals have zero oxidation state.

Reason R : Low oxidation states are found when a complex has ligands capable of $\pi$ -donor character in addition to the $\sigma$ -bonding.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below

options.label: A
options.text: is not correct but R is correct
options.html: A is not correct but R is correct

options.label: B
options.text: is correct but R is not correct
options.html: A is correct but R is not correct

options.label: C
options.text: Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
options.html: Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

options.label: D
options.text: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
options.html: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A

questions.explanation_text: Option B: "A is correct but R is incorrect" is the right answer. Here is the reasoning: Assertion A is correct. In the complex $Ni(CO)_{4}$ , if we assume the oxidation state of Ni to be x, we can set up the equation: $x+(0 \times 4)=0$ From which we find that (x = 0). Similarly, in $Fe(CO)_{5}$ , if we let the oxidation state of Fe be y, the equation becomes: $y+(0 \times 5)=0$ Solving this gives (y = 0). Therefore, the oxidation states of both Ni and Fe are zero in their respective complexes, verifying that Assertion A is true. Regarding Reason R , it is incorrect. The low oxidation states in these complexes are stabilized through synergic bonding, which involves the ligand being a $\pi$ -acceptor, not a $\pi$ -donor. The CO ligand in these complexes accepts electron density from the metal into its antibonding molecular orbitals, characterizing a $\pi$ -acid ligand, and not a $\pi$ -donor ligand as stated. Consequently, Reason R does not hold true.

questions.explanation_text: In chromyl chloride, $CrO_{2}Cl_{2}$ , the oxidation state of chromium can be calculated by assigning oxidation states to the other atoms in the molecule and then using the fact that the sum of the oxidation states in a molecule must be equal to zero. The oxidation state of oxygen is usually -2 and the oxidation state of chlorine is usually -1. Therefore, we can write: $Cr+2O(-2)+2Cl(-1)=0$ Simplifying the equation, we get: $Cr-4-2=0$ $Cr-6=0$ $Cr=+6$ Therefore, the oxidation state of chromium in chromyl chloride is $(+6)$ .

The oxidation state of oxygen is usually -2 and the oxidation state of chlorine is usually -1.

Therefore, we can write:

$Cr+2O(-2)+2Cl(-1)=0$

Simplifying the equation, we get:

$Cr-4-2=0$

$Cr-6=0$

$Cr=+6$

Therefore, the oxidation state of chromium in chromyl chloride is $(+6)$ .

An octahedral arrangement would consist of six oxygen atoms surrounding a central manganese atom, and a Mn-Mn bond would involve two manganese atoms sharing electrons without an oxygen atom in between. Neither of these are present in $Mn_{2}O_{7}$ .

The oxidation state of manganese changes from +7 in $KMnO_{4}$ to +2 in $Mn^{2+}$ , which is a reduction of 5 units. Therefore, the total change in the oxidation state of manganese involved in the reaction is $5$ .
questions.explanation_html:
The reaction of $KMnO_{4}$ and potassium iodide ( $KI$ ) in acidic medium can be represented as follows:

$MnO_{4}^{-}+I^{-}+H^{+} \rightarrow Mn^{2+}+I_{2}+H_{2}O$

In this reaction, $KMnO_{4}$ acts as an oxidizing agent, while $KI$ acts as a reducing agent. The oxidation state of manganese changes from +7 in $KMnO_{4}$ to +2 in $Mn^{2+}$ , which is a reduction of 5 units.

Therefore, the total change in the oxidation state of manganese involved in the reaction is $5$ .

$2Cu^{+} \rightarrow Cu^{+2}+Cu$

$Cu^{+1}$ disproportionates to $Cu^{+2}$ and $Cu$

questions.question_text: Which one of the lanthanoids given below is the most stable in divalent form?
questions.question_html: Which one of the lanthanoids given below is the most stable in divalent form?
questions.explanation_text: The stability of a divalent state can often be attributed to the stability of the electron configuration of that state. Among the options given, we can evaluate the electron configurations of each element in their divalent state to find out which is the most stable. The electronic configurations of the neutral atoms are : Ce (Atomic Number 58) : $[Xe]4f^{1}5d^{1}6s^{2}$ Sm (Atomic Number 62) : $[Xe]4f^{6}6s^{2}$ Eu (Atomic Number 63) : $[Xe]4f^{7}6s^{2}$ Yb (Atomic Number 70) : $[Xe]4f^{14}6s^{2}$ In their divalent state (+2 oxidation state), the electron configurations would be : Ce : $[Xe]4f^{1}5d^{1}$ (removal of the 2 electrons from the 6s orbital) Sm : $[Xe]4f^{6}$ (removal of the 2 electrons from the 6s orbital) Eu : $[Xe]4f^{7}$ (removal of the 2 electrons from the 6s orbital) Yb : $[Xe]4f^{14}$ (removal of the 2 electrons from the 6s orbital) Among these, Eu in its divalent state has a half-filled (4f) shell, which offers extra stability due to symmetrical electron distribution. Therefore, Eu (Atomic Number 63) is the most stable in the divalent form. So the correct answer is Option C : Eu (Atomic Number 63).
questions.explanation_html:
The stability of a divalent state can often be attributed to the stability of the electron configuration of that state. Among the options given, we can evaluate the electron configurations of each element in their divalent state to find out which is the most stable. The electronic configurations of the neutral atoms are :

  • Ce (Atomic Number 58) : $[Xe]4f^{1}5d^{1}6s^{2}$
  • Sm (Atomic Number 62) : $[Xe]4f^{6}6s^{2}$
  • Eu (Atomic Number 63) : $[Xe]4f^{7}6s^{2}$
  • Yb (Atomic Number 70) : $[Xe]4f^{14}6s^{2}$

In their divalent state (+2 oxidation state), the electron configurations would be :

  • Ce : $[Xe]4f^{1}5d^{1}$ (removal of the 2 electrons from the 6s orbital)
  • Sm : $[Xe]4f^{6}$ (removal of the 2 electrons from the 6s orbital)
  • Eu : $[Xe]4f^{7}$ (removal of the 2 electrons from the 6s orbital)
  • Yb : $[Xe]4f^{14}$ (removal of the 2 electrons from the 6s orbital)

Among these, Eu in its divalent state has a half-filled (4f) shell, which offers extra stability due to symmetrical electron distribution. Therefore, Eu (Atomic Number 63) is the most stable in the divalent form.

So the correct answer is Option C : Eu (Atomic Number 63).

questions.question_html:
The correct order of following 3d metal oxides, according to their oxidation numbers is :

(a) CrO3, (b) Fe2O3, (c) MnO2, (d) V2O5, (e) Cu2O
questions.explanation_text: (a) $\overset{+6}{C}rO_{3}$ : Since there are three oxygen atoms each with an oxidation number of -2, the total oxidation number from the oxygen atoms is -6. To make the compound neutral, Chromium (Cr) must therefore have an oxidation number of +6. (b) $\overset{+3}{Fe_{2}}O_{3}$ : Here, there are three oxygen atoms, contributing a total oxidation number of -6. To balance this, the total oxidation number for the two iron (Fe) atoms must be +6, meaning each Fe atom has an oxidation number of +3. (c) $\overset{+4}{Mn}O_{2}$ : With two oxygen atoms, the total oxidation number is -4. Thus, the manganese (Mn) atom must have an oxidation number of +4 to balance this. (d) $\overset{+5}{V_{2}}O_{5}$ : In this case, there are five oxygen atoms for a total oxidation number of -10. To balance this, the total oxidation number for the two vanadium (V) atoms must be +10, meaning each V atom has an oxidation number of +5. (e) $\overset{+1}{Cu_{2}}O$ : Here, there's one oxygen atom with an oxidation number of -2. To balance this, the total oxidation number for the two copper (Cu) atoms must be +2, meaning each Cu atom has an oxidation number of +1. So, the order of the oxidation numbers from highest to lowest is : (a) CrO $_{3}$ > (d) V $_{2}$ O $_{5}$ > (c) MnO $_{2}$ > (b) Fe $_{2}$ O $_{3}$ > (e) Cu $_{2}$ O. Therefore, the answer is Option C : (a) > (d) > (c) > (b) > (e).
questions.explanation_html:
(a) $\overset{+6}{C}rO_{3}$ : Since there are three oxygen atoms each with an oxidation number of -2, the total oxidation number from the oxygen atoms is -6. To make the compound neutral, Chromium (Cr) must therefore have an oxidation number of +6.

(b) $\overset{+3}{Fe_{2}}O_{3}$ : Here, there are three oxygen atoms, contributing a total oxidation number of -6. To balance this, the total oxidation number for the two iron (Fe) atoms must be +6, meaning each Fe atom has an oxidation number of +3.

(c) $\overset{+4}{Mn}O_{2}$ : With two oxygen atoms, the total oxidation number is -4. Thus, the manganese (Mn) atom must have an oxidation number of +4 to balance this.

(d) $\overset{+5}{V_{2}}O_{5}$ : In this case, there are five oxygen atoms for a total oxidation number of -10. To balance this, the total oxidation number for the two vanadium (V) atoms must be +10, meaning each V atom has an oxidation number of +5.

(e) $\overset{+1}{Cu_{2}}O$ : Here, there's one oxygen atom with an oxidation number of -2. To balance this, the total oxidation number for the two copper (Cu) atoms must be +2, meaning each Cu atom has an oxidation number of +1.

So, the order of the oxidation numbers from highest to lowest is :

(a) CrO $_{3}$ > (d) V $_{2}$ O $_{5}$ > (c) MnO $_{2}$ > (b) Fe $_{2}$ O $_{3}$ > (e) Cu $_{2}$ O.

Therefore, the answer is Option C : (a) > (d) > (c) > (b) > (e).

questions.question_html: The common positive oxidation states for an element with atomic number 24, are :

options.label: D
options.html: +1 and +3 to +6

questions.explanation_text: 24 Cr = [Ar]3d 5 4s 1 The element with atomic number 24 is Chromium (Cr). Chromium commonly exhibits several positive oxidation states, which are due to the loss of electrons from both the 4s and 3d orbitals. Here are the common oxidation states for Chromium : +2 (as in $Cr^{2+}$ ) : This is observed where the electron configuration is $[Ar]3d^{4}$ +3 (as in $Cr^{3+})$ : This is the most stable state, with the electron configuration $[Ar]3d^{3}$ +6 (as in $CrO_{4}^{2-}$ and $Cr_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-})$ : In these cases, chromium exhibits an oxidation state of +6. Hence, the common positive oxidation states for Chromium are +2, +3, and +6. Therefore, the correct option is : Option B : +2 to +6.
questions.explanation_html:
24Cr = [Ar]3d54s1

The element with atomic number 24 is Chromium (Cr). Chromium commonly exhibits several positive oxidation states, which are due to the loss of electrons from both the 4s and 3d orbitals.

Here are the common oxidation states for Chromium :

  1. +2 (as in $Cr^{2+}$ ) : This is observed where the electron configuration is $[Ar]3d^{4}$

  2. +3 (as in $Cr^{3+})$ : This is the most stable state, with the electron configuration $[Ar]3d^{3}$

  3. +6 (as in $CrO_{4}^{2-}$ and $Cr_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-})$ : In these cases, chromium exhibits an oxidation state of +6.

Hence, the common positive oxidation states for Chromium are +2, +3, and +6.

Therefore, the correct option is :

Option B : +2 to +6.

questions.explanation_text: (A) $_{58}Ce \rightarrow [Xe]4f^{2}5d^{0}6s^{2}$ In complex $Ce^{+4} \rightarrow [Xe]4f^{0}5d^{0}6s^{0}$ There is no unpaired electron, so, $\mu$ m = 0 BM (B) $_{64}Gd \rightarrow [Xe]4f^{7}5d^{1}6s^{2}$ In complex, $_{64}Gd^{2+} \rightarrow [Xe]4f^{7}5d^{1}$ There are 8 unpaired electrons. $\therefore$ $\mu_{m}=\sqrt{8(8+2)}=\sqrt{80}=8.94BM$ (C) $_{63}Eu \rightarrow [Xe]4f^{9}5d^{0}6s^{0}$ In complex $_{63}Eu^{+3} \rightarrow [Xe]4f^{6}5d^{0}6s^{0}$ contain six unpaired electrons. So, $\mu_{m}=\sqrt{6(6+2)}=\sqrt{48}BM=6.93BM$ Hence, order of spin only magnetic moment $B>C>A$ .
questions.explanation_html:
(A) $_{58}Ce \rightarrow [Xe]4f^{2}5d^{0}6s^{2}$

In complex $Ce^{+4} \rightarrow [Xe]4f^{0}5d^{0}6s^{0}$

There is no unpaired electron, so, $\mu$ m = 0 BM

(B) $_{64}Gd \rightarrow [Xe]4f^{7}5d^{1}6s^{2}$

In complex, $_{64}Gd^{2+} \rightarrow [Xe]4f^{7}5d^{1}$

There are 8 unpaired electrons.

$\therefore$ $\mu_{m}=\sqrt{8(8+2)}=\sqrt{80}=8.94BM$

(C) $_{63}Eu \rightarrow [Xe]4f^{9}5d^{0}6s^{0}$

In complex $_{63}Eu^{+3} \rightarrow [Xe]4f^{6}5d^{0}6s^{0}$

contain six unpaired electrons.

So, $\mu_{m}=\sqrt{6(6+2)}=\sqrt{48}BM=6.93BM$

Hence, order of spin only magnetic moment

$B>C>A$ .

questions.question_html: The incorrect statement is :

options.label: A
options.text:
In manganate and permanganate ions, the p-bonding takes place by overlap of p-orbitals
of oxygen and d-orbitals of manganese
options.html: In manganate and permanganate ions, the p-bonding takes place by overlap of p-orbitals of oxygen and d-orbitals of manganese

options.label: B
options.text:
Manganate ion is green in colour and
permanganate ion in purple in colour
options.html: Manganate ion is green in colour and permanganate ion in purple in colour

options.label: C

Manganate and permanganate ions are
paramagnetic
